releasePreviews.title: 2026.10 Beta: You are here 📍
releasePreviews.body:
Note

Welcome to the beta release notes for Home Assistant 2026.10 🎉

Please note that these release notes are a work in progress. 👷‍♀️ We will be
completing them over the next couple of days. Not all features might be final
yet, and some features may not make it into the final release.

Want to help test the beta? Awesome! ❤️ We have documented how you
can join our beta channel and install the beta here.

While running the beta, we highly recommend joining our #beta channel on
the Home Assistant Discord chat! 💬 Most developers and beta
testers are in this channel during the beta period to share experiences, ideas,
and iterate over new features, fine-tuning them before the final release.
It’s a really fun place to hang out. 😎

Reporting issues: As this is a beta test, you might encounter unexpected
behavior or issues. 🐞 We use the GitHub issue tracker to track beta issues.
You can find our issue trackers and the reported issues during beta here:

Report(ed) beta dashboards/UI/frontend issues

Report(ed) beta integrations/automations/backend/core issues

Report(ed) beta documentation issues

🙏 When reporting issues, make sure to mention the exact beta version you are
running in the issue description. This will help us identify and track the
issue correctly. Read more about reporting issues here.

Issues introduced in the beta are processed with priority. 🔝

Tip

Don’t forget to join our release party live stream on YouTube on October 7, 2026, at 20:00 GMT / 12:00 PT / 21:00 CET!

Home Assistant 2026.10! 🎉

Enjoy the (beta) release!

../Frenck

Need help? Join the community

All changes

A huge thank you to all the contributors who made this release possible! And a special shout-out to @frenck and @frenck who helped write these release notes. Also, @frenck, @frenck, @frenck, @frenck, and @frenck for putting effort into tweaking its contents. Thanks to them, these release notes are in great shape. ❤️

A whole new map

Last release, something changed underneath every map in Home Assistant, and we barely mentioned it in the release notes. The map provider we relied on started stamping an “API key required” message across its map images, breaking every map in Home Assistant at once. Instead of hunting for yet another free provider, we moved to OpenStreetMap. The map is now drawn from vector tiles served by the OpenStreetMap Foundation, fetched through the new Map tiles integration. Your browser never talks to a third party directly, and recently used tiles are cached, so the map keeps working through a short internet hiccup.

We did talk about it during the 2026.9 release party, where a guest from OpenStreetMap joined us. 🗺️

Swapping out the map underneath opened a lot of doors. This release walks through the first few.

Crisp at every zoom level

The map is now drawn entirely on your device, as vectors, instead of being stitched together from pictures. Streets and labels stay sharp at any zoom level, and zooming in and out is smooth. Older devices that can’t handle this, like the old tablet on your wall, automatically fall back to the classic map.

Redesigned markers

The markers on the map got a complete redesign. People show up with their picture, zones Zones allow you to specify certain regions on a map. They enable zone presence-detection and can be used in automations. For example, to start the vacuum after you left home or start the heating at home when you leave the office. [Learn more] get a marker with their icon in their own color, and everyone in the same zone shares a single bubble on that zone, instead of a pile of markers stacked on top of each other. Zoom out far enough, and bubbles that would overlap merge into one.

An overview for the Map dashboard

The Map dashboard now comes with an overview, next to the map on a desktop and as a sheet you pull up on your phone. It has three tabs: People, Devices, and Zones. Select someone to see their recent activity, with each stop colored by the zone they were in. Select a zone to see who’s there. On a phone, the map now also fills the whole screen, edge to edge.

The same overview shows up when you put a map card in a panel view on your own dashboard.

Zones on the new map

The zone editor in Settings > Areas, labels & zones now uses the same new map. Your zones are sorted alphabetically, with Home always at the top, and they show the same icons and colors you see on the map.

This is only the start. It all follows an Open Home Foundation design concept for a vector map with redesigned people and zones, and there is more of it to come. Thanks, @maartenla, @matthiasdebaat, @bramkragten, and @bgoncal!

Last but definitely not least: a big shout-out to the OpenStreetMap Foundation. 💚 OpenStreetMap is a map of the world built by millions of volunteers, and it’s open data, owned by no single company. The foundation behind it is a nonprofit that keeps it all running, including the tile servers every Home Assistant map now draws from. That fits the Open Home like a glove!

And just like Home Assistant, OpenStreetMap is made by people like you. Spot something in your neighborhood that’s missing or out of date? You can leave a note or edit the map yourself.

A tidier profile page

Select your name at the bottom of the sidebar, and you land on your User profile. Over the years, that page quietly turned into a bit of a junk drawer. Language, theme, date formats, sidebar order, push notifications, keyboard shortcuts: all stacked in one long General tab, with Security as its only neighbor. Everything was there. You just had to scroll past most of it to find the one thing you came for.

The profile page is now an overview, using the same kind of navigation you already know from Settings. At the top is a card with your account, followed by your Theme, and a short list of sections that each hold a handful of related settings:

Appearance: Your default dashboard and the order of your sidebar.

Localization: Your language, time zone, and how dates, times, and numbers are shown.

This browser (or This mobile app in the companion app): Notifications, display, and shortcuts for the device you’re using right now.

Security: Your password, multi-factor authentication, and access tokens.

Nothing was taken away. Every setting is still there, grouped so you can find what you came for. Thanks, @pcan08 and @maartenla!

That account card at the top learned a new trick, too. Until now, your own name and picture weren’t actually yours to change. Only an administrator could set them, tucked away in the person settings. Not an administrator, but wanted a nicer picture of yourself in the sidebar? You had to go ask whoever runs your Home Assistant. A bit odd, for something that is literally your face.

Every user, administrator or not, now has an Edit profile button right next to Log out. Upload and crop a picture, change your name, and save. Your name is used for both your user and the person linked to it, so it’s the same everywhere you show up, from the sidebar to your dashboards and Assist. Your new picture shows up in the sidebar right away.

The best automation feature you never used

Take a look at your automations Automations in Home Assistant allow you to automatically respond to things that happen in and around your home. [Learn more], and chances are you’ll find a few that come in pairs. One turns the hallway light on when motion is detected, the other turns it off again when the motion stops. One sends a notification when the washing machine starts, the other when it’s done. Two automations, doing one job.

Home Assistant has had a way to combine those into one for years. Give each trigger A trigger is a set of values or conditions of a platform that are defined to cause an automation to run. [Learn more] an ID, and use the Triggered by condition Conditions check whether something is true at that moment, for example, whether a door is closed. You can use them in automations and scripts. If a condition is not met, the actions that come after it in the same sequence do not run. At the top level of an automation or script, this stops the automation or script. [Learn more] to do something different depending on which trigger fired. It’s one of the most powerful things you can do in the automation editor, and also one of the best hidden. The trigger ID field sat in the menu of each trigger. You had to come up with an ID, type it in yourself, and then remember which ID belonged to which trigger when you picked them in the condition. Most people never found it, and honestly, we can’t blame them.

Not anymore. Add a Triggered by condition, and you check the triggers it should match. You see the triggers themselves, not some ID you made up, and each one is numbered by its position in your list, with the same number shown next to the trigger itself. So you always know which one is which. There are no IDs to come up with at all. Home Assistant takes care of those behind the scenes, and cleans up after itself when you remove a trigger.

If you set your trigger IDs yourself in YAML YAML is a human-readable data serialization language. It is used to store and transmit data in a structured format. In Home Assistant, YAML is used for configuration, for example in the configuration.yaml or automations.yaml files. [Learn more], those keep working exactly as they did, and you can keep setting them there. If a condition points to a trigger that no longer exists, the editor now flags it, so you can clear it. And if several triggers share the same ID, the editor warns you and offers a Fix that gives each trigger its own ID and updates your conditions to match.

This completes an Open Home Foundation roadmap opportunity to make referencing triggers in automations a lot easier. Thanks, @jpbede, @wendevlin, @marcinbauer-ohf, and @nielsrowinbik!

While you’re in the automation editor, you’ll notice your triggers, conditions, and actions tell you a bit more at a glance. Each row now shows the details that used to be hidden until you opened it: the threshold a trigger or condition checks for, like “above 10 °C”, how long something needs to stay that way, the offset on a sunrise or sunset, and how long a wait action waits before it gives up. Thanks, @wendevlin and @MindFreeze!

Integrations

Thanks to our community for keeping pace with the new integrations Integrations connect and integrate Home Assistant with your devices, services, and more. [Learn more] and improvements to existing ones! You’re all awesome 🥰

New integrations

We welcome the following new integrations in this release:

Axle Energy, added by @Herbertmt978

Bring the grid event schedule of your Axle Energy account into Home Assistant. It tells you whether an upcoming event asks you to import from or export to the grid, and exactly when it starts and ends, so your automations can get your home ready in time.

Bitvis Power Hub, added by @MandusBorjesson

Read real-time electricity data from your smart meter using a Bitvis Power Hub, which plugs into the meter’s HAN port. The Power Hub pushes its measurements, like power, voltage, and current per phase, straight to Home Assistant over your local network. No cloud, no polling Data polling is the process of querying a device or service at regular intervals to check for updates or retrieve data. By defining a custom polling interval, you can control how frequently your system checks for new data, which can help optimize performance and reduce unnecessary network traffic. [Learn more].

Gree Infrared, added by @Dr-Blank, launching at 🥈 silver quality

Control a Gree air conditioner using any infrared transmitter you already have set up in Home Assistant, like an ESPHome device with an infrared LED. Add an infrared receiver, and the climate entity follows along when someone uses the physical Gree remote. Gree builds air conditioners for many brands, so units sold as Onida, Sinclair, and others work as well.

INDI Allsky, added by @TN-1

Connect your INDI Allsky camera server, an allsky camera system for astrophotography and keeping an eye on cloud cover. You get the latest capture as a camera, plus sensors for sky quality, the number of stars detected, exposure time, and whether it’s night.

KACO Modbus, added by @g4bri3lDev

Connect a KACO new energy solar inverter directly over your local network using Modbus TCP. It shows what the inverter is producing right now, its lifetime energy counter for the Energy dashboard, and what it is doing, without any cloud account or manufacturer portal involved.

my-PV, added by @rrooggiieerr

Control my-PV devices, like the AC•THOR range and AC ELWA 2, which turn your surplus solar power into hot water. Home Assistant talks to them locally and discovers them on your network automatically.

OSRAM Infrared, added by @freeDom-, launching at 🥈 silver quality

Control OSRAM and LEDVANCE RGB lights that come with a 24-button infrared remote, using an infrared transmitter set up in Home Assistant. With an infrared receiver, the light entity also picks up commands from the physical remote.

Persang Infrared, added by @Dr-Blank

Control a Persang Bluetooth speaker using an infrared transmitter set up in Home Assistant, giving you a media player and buttons for its remote functions.

SolarEdge Modbus, added by @frenck, launching at 🏆 platinum quality

Connect to your SolarEdge solar inverter over your own network, using the Modbus TCP interface built into the inverter. No account, no API key, no cloud. Readings arrive every few seconds instead of every few minutes, and keep arriving when your internet connection is down. You can also change the export limit and how your battery charges.

Sunsynk, added by @jamesridgway

Bring your Sunsynk hybrid solar inverter and battery into Home Assistant using your Sunsynk Connect account. You get sensors for solar production, grid import and export, and your battery. Home Assistant can even discover the Sunsynk data logger on your network.

Theben Conexa Smart Meter Gateway, added by @mdluhosch

Read your meter data locally from a Theben Conexa 3.0 smart meter gateway, using its built-in Home Area Network (HAN) interface. No cloud needed.

Threema, added by @LukasQ

Send end-to-end encrypted messages from your automations to people on Threema, the privacy-focused messenger that doesn’t need a phone number. It uses the Threema Gateway service, and each person you add as a recipient gets their own notify entity.

Vitesy, added by @chemelli74

Connect the Vitesy Shelfy, an air purifier that lives in your refrigerator. See the air quality and temperature inside your fridge, how often the door was opened, and when the filter needs cleaning or replacing. You can even switch the purifier mode, for example to boost it after a grocery run.

Willow, added by @PaxPrz

Keep an eye on the health of your indoor plants with Willow sensors. Temperature, humidity, soil moisture, and light levels come from the Willow cloud into Home Assistant, ready for your dashboards and automations. Your plants can’t tell you they’re thirsty, but now Home Assistant can.

Zonneplan, added by @erwindouna

Get the electricity and gas prices of your Zonneplan contract, a Dutch provider of dynamic energy contracts. Handy for running your appliances when energy is cheapest.

This release also has new virtual integrations. Virtual integrations are stubs that are handled by other (existing) integrations to help with findability. These ones are new:

Austroflamm, provided by Fumis, added by @frenck

EcoSpar, provided by Fumis, added by @frenck

HAAS+SOHN, provided by Fumis, added by @frenck

HETA, provided by Fumis, added by @frenck

O General, provided by FGLair, added by @Dr-Blank

Onida Infrared, provided by Gree Infrared, added by @Dr-Blank

Steinway & Lyngdorf, provided by Lyngdorf, added by @fishloa

Noteworthy improvements to existing integrations

It is not just new integrations Integrations connect and integrate Home Assistant with your devices, services, and more. [Learn more] that have been added; existing ones keep getting better too. Here are some of the noteworthy improvements this release:

Matter added switches to turn the visual and audible alarms of supported leak sensors on or off, like the IKEA KLIPPBOK, and a switch for one-touch locking, so you decide whether a single touch on the keypad of your lock is enough to lock the door. Devices that measure electrical power now also report the frequency and power factor. Thanks, @wardmatter, @mmmspatz, and @lboue!

Tuya supports a lot more devices this release: two-channel DIN rail energy meters with readings per channel, circuit breakers, EV chargers (with their charging current, charging mode, and session energy), water valves (with water usage and temperature), and the keypad tone and alarm push settings of the Duosmart C30 alarm panel. Three-phase electricity meters now also report reactive power, apparent power, and power factor for each phase. Thanks, @keranm, @tmunzer, @o-borovets, @syl-craft, @ChayoteJarocho, @huangrenwei79, and @epenet!

Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) added page counters, so you can keep track of how many pages, impressions, and sheets your printer has gone through, split into color and black and white on printers that report it. Thanks, @brianegge!

ESPHome devices can now open the connection to Home Assistant themselves, so they work even when Home Assistant can’t reach them directly. Turn on the outgoing_connection option on your ESPHome device, and Home Assistant takes it from there, with the same encryption as always. Thanks, @bdraco!

HomeKit Bridge can now show your valve entities in the Home app as a faucet, shower head, or sprinkler. How long a valve runs can now also come from any number entity, not just a number helper. Thanks, @louwii17!

Philips Hue added a switch to turn each MotionAware zone on or off, just like you can in the Hue app. Rooms and zones also gained a scene select, showing which scene (or smart scene) is currently active, and letting you pick another one. Thanks, @marcelveldt and @sliekens!

Reolink can now control the pan and tilt lens of cameras that combine multiple lenses in one device, when connected to a Reolink NVR or Home Hub. Thanks, @starkillerOG!

Music Assistant announcements can now speak a message, not only play an audio file. The announcement action takes a message and a text-to-speech entity to speak it, while keeping the pre-announcement chime and announcement volume that tts.speak doesn’t offer. The AI search tool can now also search inside artists, albums, and playlists. Thanks, @marcelveldt and @balloob!

Roborock wet and dry vacuums now update in real time, so docking or starting a cleaning shows up in Home Assistant right away. The Roborock Q10 can now also clean specific zones, drive to a spot you pick, and report where it is. Thanks, @piitaya and @hmmbob!

Z-Wave added three new conditions to the automation editor, with proper fields to fill in: check a device’s node status, the value of a configuration parameter, or any other Z-Wave value. Z-Wave triggers got the same treatment. Thanks, @raman325!

UniFi Network now reports the battery level and runtime of your UniFi UPS, along with its output power, current, voltage, and power factor. Thanks, @jimstrang!

Broadlink now supports the RM5 Plus, which used to fail with a “device not supported” error. Thanks, @DAB-LABS!

UniFi Protect now supports the UniFi Protect key fob, with its battery, status, and an event entity An event entity represents a momentary occurrence without a lasting state, for example, when you press a doorbell or a button on a remote control. Instead of a state such as on or off, the event entity keeps track of when the last event was detected and its event type, such as a single press or a long press. [Learn more] for every button press, like arm, disarm, or panic, and each input of a UniFi Protect relay now shows up as its own binary sensor. The API key only mode gained camera events for motion, smart detection, sound, and packages. Thanks, @sbesh91, @igoraugustynski, and @RaHehl!

OpenAI added support for the GPT-6 Astra and GPT-Image-2.5 models. GPT-Image-2.5 Flare is now the default for generating images with AI Task. Thanks, @Shulyaka!

SwitchBot Bluetooth added support for the Lock Ultra Max, the Universal Remote, and the RGBICWW Light Bars, and lets you set how fast your SwitchBot curtains move. Thanks, @Onero-testdev and @joostlek!

SwitchBot Cloud added support for the Lock Ultra Max. Thanks, @XiaoLing-git!

LIFX now supports LIFX lights that connect over Thread Thread is a low-power mesh networking standard that is specifically designed for smart home applications. It is a protocol that defines how devices communicate. [Learn more], and the signal strength sensor works for those lights too. Thanks, @Djelibeybi!

Proxmox VE added update entities for your Proxmox nodes, showing when updates are available and how many Proxmox and other packages are waiting. Installing them from Home Assistant is not possible yet. Thanks, @CoMPaTech!

LinkPlay speakers that follow another speaker in a multiroom group now show the title, artist, album, and album art of what’s playing. Each speaker keeps its own volume. Thanks, @MagicMicky!

Apple iCloud brings your iCloud calendars and Reminders into Home Assistant. Each calendar shows up as a calendar entity, and each Reminders list as a to-do list, where you can add, complete, and remove items that sync right back to your Apple devices. Thanks, @FezVrasta!

Hikvision added event entities that tell you what triggered a smart event: a human, a vehicle, or a pet. Great for getting notified about people at your gate, while ignoring passing traffic. Thanks, @ptarjan!

Opower now uses the import and export readings from your meter itself for your grid statistics. Before, grid import was worked out from your net usage, which undercounted it for homes with solar panels, and could even show no import at all on a sunny day. Thanks, @tronikos!

TP-Link Omada now shows your Omada controller as a device, with its status and an update entity for its firmware. Thanks, @rubempoli!

EnergyZero can now use quarter-hourly electricity prices, and added all-in electricity prices next to the market prices. Thanks, @klaasnicolaas!

Bosch SHC grew a lot this release. Micromodule shutters, awnings, and blinds now show up as covers, and there are new switches for child locks, the alarm bypass of door and window contacts, the silent mode of thermostats, the intrusion alarm of the Smoke Detector II, and the settings of the Motion Detector 2, Door/Window Contact II Plus, Micromodule Relay, and Camera Eyes. Show a card only when it matters

Dashboards can show or hide a card, badge, or section based on conditions Conditions check whether something is true at that moment, for example, whether a door is closed. You can use them in automations and scripts. If a condition is not met, the actions that come after it in the same sequence do not run. At the top level of an automation or script, this stops the automation or script. [Learn more]: only on a phone, only for a certain user, only when the washing machine is running. Those conditions were always a smaller set than the ones you know from automations.

Last release, we started modernizing Modbus: integrations that already know how your device talks Modbus, so you pick your device in the UI instead of writing register maps by hand. Those integrations share a single connection to each device, which is great for devices that only accept a few connections at once. It also meant there was no single place to see which integrations were talking to what.

The new Modbus panel under Settings > Connectivity fixes that. It lists every Modbus connection Home Assistant has, serial ports and network gateways alike, along with the devices A device is a model representing a physical or logical unit that contains entities. on it and the integrations using them. Connections set up in YAML show up here too. A connection that’s closed isn’t a problem, by the way. It opens again the next time an integration needs it. The Serial panel links straight to it for ports that carry Modbus. Thanks, @balloob!

The list of integrations built this way keeps growing. This release adds two new ones: SolarEdge Modbus, launching straight at platinum, and KACO Modbus, thanks to @g4bri3lDev. Connect your AI in one click

Home Assistant can act as a Model Context Protocol server, which lets AI apps like Claude, ChatGPT, or Cursor talk to your home. Getting there was a bit of a hunt, though: add the integration, pick which parts of Home Assistant to expose, and then figure out which URL to hand to your AI app.

The AI tasks page under Settings > System is now called AI, and it gained a Model Context Protocol card. Turn the server on in a single click, and the card lists the URLs to paste into your AI app, each with a button to copy it. New setups expose everything Home Assistant has to offer, including anything added later, and only allow administrator accounts to connect. You can change both whenever you like, without removing and re-adding the integration.

It also works the other way around. Apps that run their own MCP server are now discovered automatically by the Model Context Protocol integration, so connecting Home Assistant to them only takes a confirmation.

And your AI got a lot better at finding music. Ask it to play something, and instead of blindly playing the first search result, it now gets a list of results and picks the best match. It can even search inside an artist, album, or playlist to find that one specific song. Search itself improved along the way: artists, albums, and playlists from Music Assistant can now be searched inside, just like results from Jellyfin and Squeezebox, local media now finds matching folders too, and Radio Browser puts the 100 most popular stations first.

Thanks, @balloob!

If your home runs on KNX, your AI can now dig into that too. The KNX integration brings its own set of AI tools, which you can hand to your conversation agent, or to your AI app through the Model Context Protocol server. Ask about the group addresses, devices, and functions in your ETS project, go through the history of telegrams on your bus, or decode a value you don’t recognize. It can even read and write values on the bus directly. Thanks, @martinhoefling!

Some entities An entity represents a sensor, actor, or function in Home Assistant. Entities are used to monitor physical properties or to control other entities. The switch also shows you what that device name is, with a link to rename the device if you’d like. Turn it off, and you’re back to the entity’s own name, filled in with the default from the integration. If you change your mind, a restore button takes you back to the default. Thanks, @piitaya and @matthiasdebaat!

articles.title: Home Assistant 2026.10 brings clearer maps and simpler automations
articles.dek: Today’s release makes household locations easier to read and removes the need to invent trigger identifiers.
body: Home Assistant 2026.10 arrives today with a redesigned map that makes it easier to see where people and devices are. Streets and labels stay sharp while zooming, people in the same zone share a marker, and an overview lists people, devices and zones alongside recent activity. Older devices that cannot draw the new map fall back to the classic version.

The automation editor makes a long-standing capability easier to find: one automation can respond differently to several triggers without its author inventing and remembering trigger identifiers. The Triggered by condition offers the actual triggers to select, flags missing references and helps repair shared identifiers. Existing identifiers written in YAML keep working.

Dashboards also gain the automation editor’s conditions for showing cards, badges and sections, including time-of-day, zone and template checks. The visibility editor shows whether each condition currently passes, so a hidden card is easier to explain.

Before upgrading, check automations that people start manually: publishing MQTT messages and restarting or shutting down a Synology NAS now require an administrator when a person starts the action, script or automation. Automations running from their own triggers are unaffected.

media.alt: Home Assistant map with redesigned people and zone markers

articles.title: ESPHome detects movement using an ESP32 and existing Wi-Fi
articles.dek: ESPectre joins the built-in components, with no additional sensing hardware but a clear limit on still occupants.
body: ESPHome adds motion sensing through changes in Wi-Fi signals, allowing an ESP32 and an existing access point to detect movement without a separate motion sensor. ESPectre, previously supplied as an external component, joins the built-in components with motion readings, a movement score and a recalibration button.

Francesco Pace makes his first contribution to ESPHome with the integration, tested on six ESP32 chip variants. It measures how movement changes the paths taken by the Wi-Fi signal; it cannot reliably detect a person who stays still, so no movement does not mean the room is empty.

The component disables Wi-Fi power saving and changes packet handling, which can reduce throughput for other tasks on the same device, including audio and firmware uploads. J. Nick Koston, Jesse Hills and Jonathan Swoboda reviewed the implementation.

pullRequests.title: [espectre] Add Wi-Fi CSI motion detection component
[espectre] Add ESPectre Wi-Fi motion detection documentation

articles.title: Home Assistant protects saved backups and speeds encrypted restores
articles.dek: A filename conflict stops deleting the original backup, while highly compressed restores use less processing and memory.
body: Home Assistant protects an existing backup when another backup is requested with the same filename. Previously, the new request failed but its error handler also deleted the older file, leaving it listed even though it was gone. Manuel Rüger keeps that file untouched and reports the conflict in his first contribution to Supervisor.

A separate restore correction prevents highly compressible encrypted backups, such as those containing empty database journal files, from overwhelming Supervisor. Stefan Agner reduces the size of each chunk being decompressed, limiting the large temporary buffers that could make small computers run out of memory.

In Agner’s Python 3.14 extraction test with a compressed 100 MB zero-filled file, the smaller buffer reduced processing from 32.5 seconds to 2.1 seconds. That is a specific extraction benchmark, not a promise for every full restore; unencrypted restores and backup creation keep their existing buffer settings.

Use small buffer when restoring encrypted backups

articles.title: Home Assistant’s iOS migration plan sets out a winter handover
articles.dek: The public roadmap proposes December-to-March migration dates while retaining another attempt to transfer the existing App Store listing.
body: Home Assistant’s iOS ownership plan now proposes a migration window from December 2, 2026, through March 2, 2027. The roadmap proposes an announcement for November 24 and the start of the old app’s wind-down for March 3. These are planning dates; the work remains in Building.

The proposed handover lets a foundation-published app take over the existing Home Assistant registration, preserving entity identities, notification targets and automations while the user signs in again. Another attempt to transfer the existing Apple listing remains in scope. The revised plan confirms there is no legal deadline, and the old app’s final support and removal dates remain open.

The phased approach builds on a migration outline shared by Matthias de Baat and preliminary handover work described by Bruno Pantaleão Gonçalves. The plan also needs to preserve notifications for households that install the replacement without a handover or never reopen the old app.

externalSources.title: Move companion app ownership to the foundation

articles.title: Music Assistant cuts the space needed for audio analysis
articles.dek: One tested library’s database files shrink by 87%, while a separate store preserves analysis through a library reset.
body: Music Assistant reduces the disk space used by the audio analysis behind Smart Fades and similarity-based listening. In contributor Chris’s production library of 11,600 tracks and 58,000 analysis records, the database files shrink from 3,903 MB to 523 MB—an 87% reduction. Moving and packing the records took about 30 seconds in that test.

The work gives audio analysis its own database and stores its numerical results more compactly. A library reset no longer discards that separate analysis store, and damage to the analysis database can be handled without replacing the music library. The changes also stop Smart Fades results and similarity analysis from overwriting each other.

The transfer checks the copied records before removing the originals. If it fails, the original records remain in the library database, but the transfer is not retried automatically. Marvin Schenkel reviewed the coordinated changes.

Promote audio analysis arrays to typed fields

articles.title: Music Assistant sends spoken announcements from your phone
articles.dek: Type a message or hold to talk, then send it to a household speaker.
body: Music Assistant’s Android and iPhone app gains a Play announcement control for sending a typed message or your own voice to a speaker. The speaker pauses or lowers its music for the message, then continues afterward.

Andrii Mitnovych adds a hold-to-talk button that sends the message when released, with optional chimes and a custom announcement volume. Microphone permission is requested when the button is first used, and the app does not store the recording.
Typed messages require a text-to-speech engine on the server. Spoken messages need a server supporting the live-announcement connection and cannot target the player on the same phone.

pullRequests.title: Play announcement (typed or spoken)

articles.title: ESPHome devices can initiate their connection to Home Assistant
articles.dek: Devices on restricted networks gain an encrypted route back to Home Assistant.
body: ESPHome devices gain an option to initiate their own encrypted connection instead of waiting for Home Assistant to reach them. A device can remember the last compatible client and call it back when incoming connections stop, or use a fixed destination when its network blocks incoming access.

J. Nick Koston supplies the firmware counterpart to the Home Assistant support reported on September 11. That earlier work still required compatible device firmware and an initial Home Assistant setup in which the device was reachable; the new option does not remove that setup requirement.
Encryption verifies the other end. J. Nick Koston tested successful connections and failure recovery on a D1 mini and Pico W. Jesse Hills reviewed the implementation and guide.

articles.title: Matter.js keeps separate smart-home networks’ session lists private
articles.dek: A filtering correction prevents one paired network from reading another’s sensitive list entries.
body: Devices built with Matter.js stop exposing certain sensitive list entries from one paired smart-home network to another. The affected handling includes video-session lists and certificate-related lists; a remote read previously returned entries belonging to every network instead of only the requester’s.

Ingo Fischer also removes the departed network’s entries when it is unpaired, preventing a later network that reuses its internal identifier from inheriting them. The existing WebRTC requestor already exposes session lists; some other affected list types are groundwork for implementations still to come.

pullRequests.title: fix(node): filter and purge fabric-sensitive list attributes

articles.title: Matter.js respects locks that prohibit remote unlocking
articles.dek: Lockout and operating-mode rules apply even to commands that omit a PIN.
body: Locks built with Matter.js reject remote operations when their operating mode prohibits them, closing a path that previously allowed a controller to select “No remote lock or unlock” and then unlock remotely anyway. Commands without a PIN also stop bypassing a wrong-code lockout.

Ingo Fischer extends authorization beyond the timed PIN access reported on October 6: the prohibition on remote control and the wrong-code lockout apply even when a command supplies no PIN. Users marked as having no access are refused, and disposable access ends after one successful unlock. These are rules for lock implementations built with the library; local keypad and fingerprint handling remain separate.

pullRequests.title: fix(node): authorize every Door Lock operation and add a hardware hook

articles.title: Music Assistant connects new Sendspin players alongside older ones
articles.dek: The server adopts the release-candidate protocol while retaining compatibility with existing web and Chromecast players.
body: Music Assistant implements Sendspin’s 1.0 release-candidate protocol, providing the server connection needed by clients using the revised pairing and encrypted-connection design. This completes the Music Assistant side of the C++ client change reported on October 2, while retaining compatibility with older players.

Maxim Raznatovski adapts the Music Assistant provider, with dynamic pairing codes always six digits. Existing web, Chromecast and MSX players remain compatible. Synchronized changes of track titles and artwork remain separate work. Marvin Schenkel reviewed the implementation.

pullRequests.title: Update Sendspin to 1.0.0-rc1

articles.title: Home Assistant limits idle access to apps opened from its sidebar
articles.dek: Repeated requests stop extending an app’s access window by hours or days.
body: Home Assistant’s Supervisor corrects how sessions for apps opened through its interface expire. Every request had added another fifteen minutes to the existing deadline, so a page loading about a hundred files could push expiry roughly twenty-five hours into the future.

Manuel Rüger changes the deadline to fifteen minutes after the most recent request. Active use continues to refresh the session, while fifteen minutes without requests lets it expire instead of preserving an ever-growing access window.

pullRequests.title: Use a sliding expiry window for ingress sessions

articles.title: Assist speaks its first answer after a long silence
articles.dek: Voice devices using server-side wake-word detection stop losing the reply after five quiet minutes.
body: Assist corrects a failure that could leave a voice device silent on the first request after more than five minutes without speech. Devices waiting for Home Assistant to detect a wake word could receive an answer whose audio link had already expired; repeating the question immediately worked.

Franck Nijhof makes the speech stream’s expiry count from when its answer is produced. Producing the answer also restores a stream already removed from the temporary store, keeping its audio available for the device to fetch.

pullRequests.title: Keep a TTS stream available once its message is set

articles.title: Home Assistant controls both sides of LIFX Ceiling and Mirror lights
articles.dek: Separate controls adjust the uplight and downlight, or the mirror’s front and back.
body: LIFX Ceiling and Mirror owners gain separate Home Assistant controls for the different parts of their lights. Ceiling devices expose their uplight and downlight, while Mirror devices expose their front and back, allowing different brightness and colour choices within one fixture.
The Mirror also gains a Color Sweep effect through a chosen palette. Firmware effects still apply to the whole device.

pullRequests.title: Add LIFX Ceiling and Mirror component lights and the Color Sweep effect

articles.title: Music Assistant keeps household Tidal favourites separate
articles.dek: Connecting a second account stops replacing the first account’s favourites playlist.
body: Music Assistant keeps each Tidal account’s Favorite Tracks playlist as a separate library entry. Previously, adding a second account could take over the first account’s playlist because both use the same internal playlist name.

Marvin Schenkel’s correction also covers the equivalent personal playlists in Yandex Music and KION Music. Playlists already combined need to be removed from the library and synchronized again; the correction does not split them automatically.

pullRequests.title: Keep favorite tracks of multiple Tidal accounts apart in the library

articles.title: Home Assistant keeps WLED colours and white light in step
articles.dek: Compatible strips gain combined colour and warm-white/cool-white control instead of a colour wheel that snaps back.
body: Home Assistant corrects how it controls WLED strips that combine colour with white light. The colour wheel could jump back to white because the reported mode stayed fixed, while changing colour temperature could do nothing when the white channel was off. The connection now follows the light’s actual colour and enables the white channel when setting its temperature.

Strips with separate warm-white and cool-white LEDs also gain combined colour and white control, using the LED configuration reported by WLED to split the white correctly. After changing a strip’s LED type in WLED, reload the Home Assistant integration so it picks up the new capabilities.

Fix color and white control of WLED lights with warm and cold white

articles.title: Music Assistant stops its web player jumping to full volume
articles.dek: The browser keeps the chosen level between sessions and after a lost connection.
body: Music Assistant’s web player remembers its volume instead of starting every new session at 100%. Pressing play the next day or reconnecting after a lost server connection no longer raises it unexpectedly to full volume.
OzGav stores the level in the browser and restores it before the player connects. Mute is not carried into a new session. Contributor stvncode reviewed the correction.

articles.title: Home Assistant brings monthly Monarch Money budgets onto dashboards
articles.dek: Each category shows the actual amount, the planned amount and the budget remaining.
body: Home Assistant adds monthly budget readings from Monarch Money alongside its existing account information. Each budget category has sensors for the actual amount, planned amount and amount remaining, including any rollover reported by Monarch Money.
Bradley Florence makes newly added categories appear during the normal four-hour refresh. A category without data for the current month reports unavailable instead of showing an old month’s budget.
